paragraphs: Call me Ishmael. Some years ago, never mind exactly how long, I had little or no money and nothing in particular to interest me on land, so I thought I would sail around a little and see the watery part of the world. It’s my way of driving off the blues and getting my blood moving. Whenever I find myself growing grim around the mouth, whenever it’s a damp, drizzly November in my soul, whenever I catch myself pausing in front of coffin warehouses and trailing along at the end of every funeral I meet, and especially whenever my gloom gets such a hold on me that it takes strong moral principle to keep me from deliberately stepping into the street and knocking people’s hats off, then I decide it’s high time to get to sea as soon as I can. That’s my substitute for the pistol and the bullet. With a philosophical flourish, Cato throws himself on his sword. I quietly take to the ship. There’s nothing surprising in this. If they only knew it, almost all men, at some time or other, feel very nearly the same way about the ocean that I do.

Look at the island city of Manhattan, ringed by wharves the way tropical islands are ringed by coral reefs, with commerce breaking around it like surf. Left and right, the streets lead you toward the water. At its southern tip is the Battery, where that noble breakwater is washed by waves and cooled by breezes that a few hours earlier were out of sight of land. Look at the crowds of water-gazers there.

Walk around the city on a dreamy Sunday afternoon. Go from Corlears Hook to Coenties Slip, and from there north along Whitehall. What do you see? Posted like silent sentinels all around the town stand thousands upon thousands of men lost in dreams of the sea. Some lean against the pilings, some sit on the ends of piers, some look over the rails of ships from China, and some are high up in the rigging, as if trying to get an even better view out to sea. But these are all landsmen, who on weekdays are shut up in lath and plaster, tied to counters, nailed to benches, clamped to desks. How can this be? Are the green fields gone? What are they doing here?

But look! Here come more crowds, heading straight for the water and seemingly ready to dive in. Strange! Nothing will satisfy them but the very edge of the land. Loitering in the shade of those warehouses won’t do. No. They have to get as near the water as they can without falling in. And there they stand, miles of them, leagues of them. All of them inlanders, they come from lanes and alleys, streets and avenues, north, east, south, and west. Yet here they all come together. Tell me, does the magnetic pull of the compass needles of all those ships draw them there?

Once more. Say you’re in the country, in some high land of lakes. Take almost any path you like, and ten to one it leads you down into a valley and leaves you by a pool in a stream. There’s magic in it. Let the most absent-minded man be plunged in his deepest daydream. Stand that man on his feet, set him walking, and he’ll lead you unfailingly to water, if there’s any water in the whole region. If you’re ever thirsty in the great American desert, try this experiment, as long as your caravan happens to include a professor of metaphysics. Yes, as everyone knows, meditation and water are married forever.

But here is an artist. He wants to paint you the dreamiest, shadiest, quietest, most enchanting bit of romantic landscape in the whole valley of the Saco. What is the main element he uses? There stand his trees, each with a hollow trunk, as if a hermit and a crucifix were inside, and here sleeps his meadow, and there sleep his cattle, and up from that cottage goes a sleepy smoke. Deep into the distant woods winds a mazy path, reaching to overlapping mountain spurs bathed in the blue of the hillside. But though the picture lies thus entranced, and though this pine tree shakes down its sighs like leaves onto the shepherd’s head, it would all be in vain unless the shepherd’s eye were fixed on the magic stream before him. Go visit the prairies in June, when for scores upon scores of miles you wade knee-deep among tiger lilies. What is the one charm missing? Water. There isn’t a drop of water there! If Niagara were just a cataract of sand, would you travel a thousand miles to see it? Why did the poor poet of Tennessee, upon suddenly receiving two handfuls of silver, debate whether to buy himself a coat, which he sadly needed, or spend his money on a walking trip to Rockaway Beach? Why is almost every strong, healthy boy with a strong, healthy soul in him, at some time or other, crazy to go to sea? Why, on your first voyage as a passenger, did you yourself feel such a mystical shiver when you were first told that you and your ship were now out of sight of land? Why did the ancient Persians hold the sea sacred? Why did the Greeks give it its own god, own brother of Jove? Surely all this isn’t without meaning. And the meaning goes deeper still in the story of Narcissus, who, because he couldn’t grasp the tormenting, gentle image he saw in the fountain, plunged into it and drowned. But that same image we ourselves see in all rivers and oceans. It is the image of the ungraspable phantom of life, and that is the key to it all.

Now, when I say that I’m in the habit of going to sea whenever I begin to get hazy about the eyes and overly aware of my lungs, I don’t mean to suggest that I ever go to sea as a passenger. To go as a passenger you need a purse, and a purse is just a rag unless you have something in it. Besides, passengers get seasick, grow quarrelsome, don’t sleep at night, and generally don’t enjoy themselves much. No, I never go as a passenger. And though I’m something of a salt, I never go to sea as a Commodore, or a Captain, or a Cook. I leave the glory and distinction of such offices to those who like them. For my part, I detest all honorable, respectable labors, trials, and tribulations of every kind whatsoever. It’s as much as I can do to take care of myself, without taking care of ships, barques, brigs, schooners, and what not. And as for going as cook (though I admit there’s considerable glory in that, a cook being a sort of officer on board ship), somehow I never fancied broiling fowls. Although once a fowl is broiled, judiciously buttered, and judiciously salted and peppered, nobody speaks more respectfully, not to say reverently, of a broiled fowl than I do. It’s out of the idolatrous doting of the old Egyptians on broiled ibis and roasted hippopotamus that you can see the mummies of those creatures in their huge bakehouses, the pyramids.

No, when I go to sea, I go as a plain sailor, right before the mast, straight down into the forecastle, and aloft to the royal masthead. True, they order me around a good deal and make me jump from spar to spar like a grasshopper in a May meadow. And at first this sort of thing is unpleasant enough. It touches your sense of honor, especially if you come from an old, established family in the land, the Van Rensselaers, or Randolphs, or Hardicanutes. And more than anything, if just before putting your hand in the tar pot, you’ve been lording it over a country schoolhouse, making the tallest boys stand in awe of you. The change is a sharp one, I assure you, from schoolmaster to sailor, and it takes a strong dose of Seneca and the Stoics to help you grin and bear it. But even this wears off in time.

What does it matter if some old skinflint of a sea captain orders me to get a broom and sweep the decks? What does that indignity amount to when weighed, I mean, on the scales of the New Testament? Do you think the archangel Gabriel thinks any less of me because I promptly and respectfully obey that old skinflint in that particular case? Who isn’t a slave? Tell me that. Well, then, however the old sea captains may order me around, however they may thump and punch me, I have the satisfaction of knowing it’s all right, that everybody else is served in much the same way, whether physically or spiritually, and so the universal thump is passed around, and all hands should rub each other’s shoulder blades and be content.

Again, I always go to sea as a sailor because they make a point of paying me for my trouble, whereas they never pay passengers a single penny that I’ve ever heard of. On the contrary, passengers themselves have to pay. And there’s all the difference in the world between paying and being paid. The act of paying is perhaps the most uncomfortable punishment that the two orchard thieves brought down on us. But being paid, what compares with it? The graceful eagerness with which a man receives money is really marvelous, considering that we so earnestly believe money to be the root of all earthly evil and that on no account can a rich man enter heaven. Ah! How cheerfully we consign ourselves to damnation!

Finally, I always go to sea as a sailor because of the healthy exercise and pure air of the forecastle deck. In this world headwinds are far more common than tailwinds (that is, if you never violate the Pythagorean maxim), and so for the most part the Commodore on the quarterdeck gets his air secondhand from the sailors in the forecastle. He thinks he breathes it first, but not so. In much the same way the common people lead their leaders in many other things, while the leaders hardly suspect it. But why it was that after repeatedly smelling the sea as a merchant sailor I should now take it into my head to go on a whaling voyage, the invisible police officer of the Fates, who keeps constant watch over me and secretly dogs my steps and influences me in some unaccountable way, can answer better than anyone. And no doubt my going on this whaling voyage was part of the grand program of Providence drawn up a long time ago. It came in as a sort of brief interlude and solo between more extensive performances. I take it that this part of the program must have read something like this:
“Grand Contested Election for the Presidency of the United States. WHALING VOYAGE BY ONE ISHMAEL. BLOODY BATTLE IN AFGHANISTAN.”

Though I can’t say exactly why those stage managers, the Fates, cast me in this shabby part of a whaling voyage when others were given magnificent parts in high tragedies, and short, easy parts in elegant comedies, and jolly parts in farces, yet now that I recall all the circumstances, I think I can see a little into the springs and motives which, cunningly presented to me in various disguises, led me to set about playing the part I did, besides tricking me into the illusion that it was a choice resulting from my own unbiased free will and discerning judgment.

Chief among these motives was the overwhelming idea of the great whale himself. Such a portentous and mysterious monster roused all my curiosity. Then there were the wild and distant seas where he rolled his island bulk, the unspeakable, nameless perils of the whale, and all the accompanying marvels of a thousand Patagonian sights and sounds. These helped to sway me to my wish. With other men, perhaps, such things wouldn’t have been inducements, but as for me, I’m tormented by an everlasting itch for things remote. I love to sail forbidden seas and land on barbarous coasts. Not ignoring what is good, I’m quick to spot a horror, and could still be sociable with it, if they’d let me, since it’s only wise to be on friendly terms with all the inmates of the place where you lodge.

For these reasons, then, the whaling voyage was welcome. The great floodgates of the wonder-world swung open, and in the wild fancies that swayed me to my purpose, two by two there floated into my innermost soul endless processions of the whale, and in the midst of them all, one grand hooded phantom, like a snow hill in the air.
